outcome: No exact value of M(n) for any n ≥ 10 has been published since 26 January 2024; the exact values stop at n = 9. In 2026 two preprints gave statistical estimates of M(10) ≈ 8.93×10⁷⁸ (Chen et al., arXiv:2606.09795; Fihman, Van Hirtum and Plessl, arXiv:2607.08446), and the Fihman preprint also estimates D(11) and D(12); none of these is an exact value.
problem_asks: The exact values of the Dedekind numbers M(n) (the number of monotone Boolean functions of n variables, equivalently the number of antichains of subsets of an n-element set, with M(0)=2, M(1)=3, M(2)=6, ...) for every n ≥ 10. Parts: (1) the exact value of M(10); (2) the exact value of M(11); (3) the exact value of M(n) for each further n ≥ 10, an infinite family, so a full answer is a value for every such n (a closed form, or an algorithm that yields each value, would settle all of them at once). The bullet asks for values, not bounds, estimates or asymptotics.

events.what_happened: Preprint arXiv:2607.08446, 'Statistical Estimation of higher Dedekind Numbers' by Alex Fihman, Lennart Van Hirtum and Christian Plessl, submitted 9 Jul 2026 (one version, v1). Gives statistical (sampling-based) estimates of D(10) through D(15), with the abstract claiming about 4 digits for D(10) and 2 digits for D(15). Three methods: buffer/pair matching on 9-variable monotone Boolean functions, Reference Subsets, and 'Weight Layer Branching' (the paper's best method, covering D(10) to D(15)). Compute stated in the body: Reference Subsets 40,000 experiments of about 6.5 s CPU each (single thread); Weight Layer Branching n=10 run takes 6.1 d. The paper states it is submitted to Journal of Computational Algebra; I found no acceptance record.
events.revisions: v1 only, submitted 9 Jul 2026 (arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Estimates, not values. D(10): Reference Subsets ≈ 8.93345×10⁷⁸ (S.E. 2.44×10⁷⁴, eq. 17; Tables 1 and 11); pair matching at block size 10⁷ gives 8.93782×10⁷⁸ (S.E. 2.234×10⁷⁵; Tables 10 and 11); Weight Layer Branching gives 8.93708404×10⁷⁸ (S.E. 3.08476142×10⁷⁵; Tables 11 and 14). An earlier buffer-based preliminary run gives 8.92(41)×10⁷⁸ (σ 2.3×10⁷⁶; Section 4.2). D(11) ≈ 3.6325×10¹⁴⁴ (S.E. 7.16×10¹⁴¹) and D(12) ≈ 7.1911×10²⁸³ (S.E. 3.25×10²⁸¹), from Section 4.3 eqs. 18 and 19 as read through the fetch tool. D(13) to D(15) are claimed at 2-digit precision; I did not retrieve their values. The paper's table of earlier D(10) values gives Korshunov's asymptotic estimate as 8.55613×10⁷⁸ (Table 3; −4.22% relative). Restriction: every number is a statistical estimate whose stated S.E. is a sampling error; none is an exact integer.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: exact M(10), exact M(11), and exact M(n) for every n ≥ 10.
events.doubts: (1) The stated S.E.s are sampling errors only. The three D(10) central values differ from one another by 4.37×10⁷⁵ (pair matching minus Reference Subsets) and 3.63×10⁷⁵ (Weight Layer Branching minus Reference Subsets). The first is about 18 times the Reference Subsets S.E. of 2.44×10⁷⁴, so at least one of the stated S.E.s understates the true error. (2) In the pair-matching table the estimate drifts with block size from 8.93402×10⁷⁸ (block 10⁵) to 8.93782×10⁷⁸ (block 10⁷), a shift of about 3.8×10⁷⁵, comparable to a single row's S.E. (about 2.3×10⁷⁵). (3) None of the three central values lies inside the ±0.0010 band (×10⁷⁸) that Chen et al. quote for M(10), yet the paper calls Chen et al.'s estimate 'consistent with our results'. (4) The paper's accuracy claims rest on sampling; I did not check the code or any error analysis beyond the tables.
events.direction: Cuts neither way against the statement: it estimates the unknown quantity M(10) (≈ 8.93×10⁷⁸) and states no exact value and no claim of exactness. It says nothing about whether any M(n) with n ≥ 10 is determined exactly.

events.what_happened: Preprint arXiv:2606.09795, 'Finite-n Estimate of Dedekind Numbers by Layer-Ratio Monte Carlo' by Tian-Shun Chen, Hao Feng, Haozhe Wang and Kilar Zhang (v2 adds Chian-Shu Chen). v1 submitted 8 Jun 2026; v2 3 Aug 2026. The abstract gives the 'protocol estimate' M̂(10) = (8.9360 ± 0.0010)×10⁷⁸. The method is a layer-ratio Monte Carlo estimator on the Whitney numbers of the downset lattice, calibrated on the known values M(8) and M(9).
events.revisions: v1 8 Jun 2026 (abstract already carries the M(10) estimate); v2 3 Aug 2026 (adds author Chian-Shu Chen; full text read for v2 only).
events.delivers: An estimate of M(10) only: 8.9360×10⁷⁸. The ± is described in the abstract as 'the budget-based forecast scale from the cross-n scaling law under the production budget'. Section 3.2 gives a seed-level standard error of 5.3089×10⁻⁵ in log₁₀ units, a bootstrap interval of 78.951143 ± 1.04×10⁻⁴, and a budget forecast of 78.951143 ± 5.0456×10⁻⁵. Calibration: log₁₀ error −6.2×10⁻⁷ at n = 8 and −5.2×10⁻⁶ at n = 9, both 'within the measured seed-level variability'. Restriction: an estimate for n = 10 from a protocol calibrated on n = 8 and 9; the paper states 'no exact value is available' for M(10). It also produces estimates at other n (not read in detail).
events.remains: All of problem_asks: exact M(10), exact M(11), and exact M(n) for every n ≥ 10.
events.doubts: (1) The ± in the headline value is a forecast scale from a cross-n scaling law, not a statistical error bar. Section 3.2 says the seed, jackknife and bootstrap measures 'do not account for systematic effects shared across seeds'. (2) The Fihman et al. central values (8.93345, 8.93708 and 8.93782, ×10⁷⁸) each lie outside this paper's stated band 8.9350 to 8.9370 (×10⁷⁸), so the two estimates disagree at the scale of their own stated uncertainties, even though Fihman et al. call them consistent. (3) The only validation is backtesting on n = 8 and 9, where the answers are known; this checks the protocol at those n, not at n = 10. (4) I read the v2 full text (via a summarising fetch) but only the abstract page for v1.
events.direction: Cuts neither way against the statement: a numerical estimate of M(10) ≈ 8.936×10⁷⁸, with no exact value and no claim of one.

events.what_happened: Preprint arXiv:2304.00895, 'A computation of the ninth Dedekind Number' by Christian Jäkel (TU Dresden), v1 3 Apr 2023, v2 5 Apr 2023. Computes M(9) = 286386577668298411128469151667598498812366 by matrix multiplication and symmetry reduction in the free distributive lattice (symmetries from formal concept analysis and nauty). Run on Nvidia A100 GPUs: 5311 GPU hours and 4257682565 matrix multiplications (the fetched text repeats these figures; read as 5311 and 4257682565). A step is stated to run on an AWS c6i.32xlarge cluster (128 cores). Neighbouring result: n = 9 is outside the bullet, which asks about n ≥ 10.
events.revisions: v1 3 Apr 2023; v2 5 Apr 2023 ('isomorphic interval definition fixed'). OEIS A000372 and Wikipedia cite it as published in Journal of Computational Algebra vol. 6–7 (2023), art. 100006; I did not open the journal page and could not confirm the publication.
events.delivers: Exact M(9) only. Restricted to n = 9; says nothing about M(n) for n ≥ 10.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: exact M(10), M(11), and every further M(n), n ≥ 10.

events.what_happened: Preprint arXiv:2405.20904, 'Solving systems of equations on antichains for the computation of the ninth Dedekind Number' by Patrick De Causmaecker and Lennart Van Hirtum, v1 31 May 2024 through v4 14 Oct 2024. Studies four systems of equations on antichains and a generalised P-coefficient. Its Theorem 6.1 and corollary 6.2 were the basis of the D(9) computation. The conclusion speculates that D(10) 'may' become computable 'between now and 2050'. It gives no value or bound for any n ≥ 10.
events.revisions: v1 31 May 2024; v2 5 Jun 2024; v3 18 Jun 2024; v4 14 Oct 2024 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Identities for counting antichain solutions to four systems of equations, and a generalised P-coefficient that the authors used for the n = 9 computation. Restricted to n = 9 in its results; no value, bound or asymptotic for n ≥ 10.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: exact M(10), M(11), and every further M(n), n ≥ 10.
events.direction: Not about the bullet. It is a method paper for n = 9 that states no n ≥ 10 result.

events.what_happened: Preprint arXiv:2411.03400, 'On Dedekind's problem, a sparse version of Sperner's theorem, and antichains of a given size in the Boolean lattice' by Matthew Jenssen, Alexandru Malekshahian and Jinyoung Park. Uses cluster expansion to give asymptotic estimates of ψ(n), the number of antichains in B_n (equal to M(n)). Intro states 'the exact value of ψ(n) is known only for n ≤ 9'.
events.delivers: Asymptotic results only. Theorem 1.1 (attributed to Korshunov and Sapozhenko) gives ψ(n) = (1+o(1))·2^N with N = C(n, ⌊n/2⌋). Theorem 1.4 refines the relative error to 2^(−tn/2)·n^O(t). Theorem 1.7 gives ψ(n) = (1+e^(−Ω(n²)))·Z(C_n,1), where C_n is the union of the central layers. A sparse Sperner threshold is also determined. No numerical value of M(n) is given for any n, including n ≥ 10. Read from the first 100,000 characters of roughly 190,000.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the exact values for every n ≥ 10. The results are approximations for large n and fix no individual value.
events.direction: Neither for nor against exact values. It gives large-n asymptotics for the same quantity and states that exact values are not known beyond n = 9.

events.what_happened: Preprint arXiv:2403.03703, 'Decomposing Dedekind Numbers: A Polynomial Representation with Powers of 2' by YongQing Liu (single author), v1 6 Mar 2024, v2 9 Mar 2024. The abstract says Dedekind numbers 'can be expressed as polynomials of powers of 2'. Main Theorem 1 is a partition identity D(S) = Σ over f in M(A) of D(S − S_A, (f(a_1),…,f(a_k))), and Corollary 1 gives D_n = D(Eⁿ − S_{a,1}) + D(Eⁿ − S_{a,0}). The introduction says 'we are actively exploring the determination of coefficients for these terms'.
events.delivers: A recursive decomposition valid for every n that expresses M(n) through smaller counts. No explicit closed form: the coefficients are not determined, and the 'powers of 2' representation claimed in the abstract is not shown in the main theorem as read. No numerical value of any M(n) is stated, including n ≥ 10.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: exact M(10), M(11), and every further M(n), n ≥ 10.
events.doubts: Single author; a 7 KB preprint with no refereeing found. The abstract claims a polynomial in powers of 2; the main decomposition theorem, as read, does not display that form, and the paper says the coefficients are not yet determined. A search summary (not opened) says the earlier Wiedemann and Jäkel computations already used a related isomorphism-based recursion (D_9 = (D_5)^(B^4)), so the decomposition may not be new. I did not confirm that by comparison.
events.direction: Neither: a structural identity that does not yield any value.

events.what_happened: Preprint arXiv:2602.04533, 'A matrix approach to the structure, enumeration, and applications of partially ordered sets' by Gi-Sang Cheon, Hong Joon Choi, Gukwon Kwon, Hojoon Lee and Yaling Wang, submitted 4 Feb 2026. Encodes naturally labelled posets as Boolean lower-triangular 'poset matrices', treating the Birkhoff and Dedekind (antichain) problems in one framework. The abstract page reports no new Dedekind number values.
events.delivers: A reformulation of antichain counting in matrix terms. No new value, bound or asymptotic for M(n) is visible on the abstract page. Discounted as a method paper; I did not read the full text.
events.direction: Neither: a reformulation of the counting problem with no value attached.

events.what_happened: Korshunov's asymptotic solution of Dedekind's problem, 'Solution of Dedekind's problem on the number of monotonic Boolean functions' (Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR 233:4, 1977, pp. 543–546, per a secondary listing). A 1981 Korshunov paper 'On the number of monotone Boolean functions' (Problemy Kibernetiki) is cited for the same asymptotics, so the dates conflict. The primary papers were not read. Fihman et al.'s Table 3 uses this asymptotic to give D(10) ≈ 8.55613×10⁷⁸ and calls Korshunov's asymptotics 'the only available estimates for D(10) and beyond' before 2026.
events.revisions: Dates conflict: 1977 (Doklady, secondary listing) vs 1981 (Problemy Kibernetiki, cited by Jenssen et al. and others).
events.delivers: An asymptotic formula for M(n), giving the approximate value 8.556×10⁷⁸ for M(10). Not an exact value.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: exact values for every n ≥ 10.

events.what_happened: Kleitman's 1969 upper bound on log M(n), improved by Kleitman and Markowsky (1975, Trans. AMS 213, 373–390). The bound shows log₂M(n) is C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) up to a factor 1+O(log n / n). The elementary Sperner-type lower bound M(n) ≥ 2^C(n,⌊n/2⌋) gives M(10) ≥ 2²⁵² ≈ 7.24×10⁷⁵, which is quoted in John D. Cook's 2023 post (opened). The trivial upper bound M(10) < 2^(2^10) ≈ 1.8×10³⁰⁸ also holds. Primary papers were not read.
events.revisions: 1969 upper bound (Kleitman); 1975 improvement (Kleitman and Markowsky), per secondary sources.
events.delivers: Bounds only: 7.24×10⁷⁵ ≤ M(10) < 1.8×10³⁰⁸ (the lower bound from the middle-layer antichain argument; the upper bound from counting all Boolean functions). These do not determine M(10).

disputes.summary: News and aggregator pages disagree on the D(9) computation: Earth.com describes conventional cluster machines and about a month of wall-clock time for Jäkel, while Jäkel's arXiv text says A100 GPUs. The primary arXiv text is used here. Some secondary pages also date the D(9) result to December 2025, which is a republication of the 2023 result. Not a priority dispute.

summary: I ran 34 searches covering the problem name and its alternative forms (Dedekind number, monotone Boolean functions, antichains, D(n), ψ(n)), result wording, recent work on the sequence, and AI terms, and opened the primary arXiv pages and HTML for every paper that matters. Exact values are known only for n ≤ 9: OEIS A000372 lists terms only through a(9), Wikipedia's table ends at n = 9, Jenssen, Malekshahian and Park (Nov 2024) state that the exact value of ψ(n) is known only for n ≤ 9, Chen et al. (v2, §3.2) say no exact value of M(10) is available, and Fihman et al. describe D(10) as unknown. Within the window there are two new events, both estimates rather than values. Chen et al. (arXiv:2606.09795, 8 Jun 2026) give M̂(10) = (8.9360 ± 0.0010)×10⁷⁸, where the ± is a forecast scale, not a statistical error. Fihman, Van Hirtum and Plessl (arXiv:2607.08446, 9 Jul 2026) give statistical estimates of D(10) ≈ 8.93345×10⁷⁸, 8.93708×10⁷⁸ and 8.93782×10⁷⁸ from three methods, and also estimates for D(11) and D(12); the paper calls the Chen et al. estimate consistent with its own, although none of its three central values lies inside Chen's stated band. Neither paper has been published in a journal that I could find (Fihman lists Journal of Computational Algebra as its target), and nobody besides the authors has engaged with either method. The two estimates agree to within about 0.05%, and both are about 4% above Korshunov's asymptotic value of 8.556×10⁷⁸. Close call: whether a four-significant-digit estimate of M(10) 'moves' the quantity the bullet asks for. The bullet asks for values, and an estimate is not a value, so I record it as no resolution; the strongest opposing reading is that the estimates pin one of the named quantities to four digits. Neighbouring n = 9 results (Jäkel and Van Hirtum et al., both April 2023; De Causmaecker and Van Hirtum, May 2024) are recorded as out-of-scope events, and the 2023 Paderborn paper was published in ACM TRETS in 2024 (ACM page returned 403; repository record used). Discounted events, each with its reason in delivers: Liu (2024, decomposition with undetermined coefficients, and the 'powers of 2' form does not appear in the main theorem as read), Jenssen et al. (2024, asymptotics only), Cheon et al. (2026, method), and Pawelski (2023, unlabelled counts at n = 9). AI: across all sources I found exactly one AI disclosure relevant to this problem, in Fihman et al.: 'During the preparation of this work the authors used ChatGPT v.5.5 for final proofreading.' Under §5.4 this is proofreading, not load-bearing, so ai.systems is empty and none_found is false. None of the 34 searches linked any AI system (AlphaEvolve, FunSearch, GPT, Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, DeepMind, LLM) to Dedekind numbers. The AI-assisted counterexamples my searches surfaced concern other Boolean-function conjectures (NICD with erasures, the most informative Boolean function conjecture) and are not recorded here. Corrections to search summaries: one snippet attributed 3.63437×10¹⁴⁴ to D(10) from Fihman et al.; the paper's body gives D(11) ≈ 3.6325×10¹⁴⁴ and D(10) ≈ 8.93×10⁷⁸. Unverified leads not recorded as events: John D. Cook's 2023 heuristic guess M(10) ≈ 3.25×10⁸² (a guess, not a result), and a secondary report of Jäkel guessing D(10) ≈ 10⁸² (source not identified). Caveat on quotes: every full text was obtained through a summarising fetch tool, so quoted sentences are the tool's output and should be checked against the source before any downstream use; the fetch tool could not decode several PDF bodies, so I relied on the HTML versions.
competing_reading: The 2026 estimates pin M(10) to about four significant digits, which some would count as a partial answer on the one named case (n = 10) and as moving a quantity the bullet asks for. The bullet asks for values, and an approximation with a non-statistical ± (Chen et al.) or a sampling S.E. that does not reconcile with the other methods (Fihman et al.) is not a value. Under the alternative reading, the bullet is not moved at all, because no exact M(n) with n ≥ 10 has appeared.
what_would_settle_it: An exact M(10) computed by a method independent of the P-coefficient/FPGA and matrix/GPU routes, and confirmed by a second independent computation, as happened for M(9) in 2023. Failing that: a peer-reviewed publication of the Fihman et al. or Chen et al. estimates with an explicit systematic-error budget, or an independent replication that reconciles the three Fihman central values with each other and with Chen's band. For the general bullet: a closed form or algorithm that yields every M(n), n ≥ 10.

Lean or Coq formalisation of Dedekind numbers: no source found.
arXiv:2608.23661 (Cerf, θ(p_c, Z^d) = 0?) appeared for a 2026 monotone Boolean query; it is a percolation paper and has nothing to do with this problem. Opened to confirm.

arXiv:2607.24832 (Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS) appeared on an AI-declaration query; it is about OEIS conjectures (totient, Fibonacci sums) and does not mention Dedekind numbers; search snippet only, not opened.
arXiv:2304.14069 (Biswas and Sarkar, counting unate and balanced monotone Boolean functions, April 2023): a different quantity; search snippet only, not opened.
arXiv:1209.4623 (counting inequivalent monotone Boolean functions, 2012) and arXiv:2108.13997 (inequivalent functions): unlabelled counts, not M(n); not opened.

arXiv:2310.12946 (Dedekind's problem in the hypergrid) and arXiv:2311.11744 (counting interval sizes in the poset of monotone Boolean functions): not opened; both appear to concern related but different quantities.
Pawelski 2024 Gdańsk doctoral dissertation (bip.ug.edu.pl) and its 2025 reviews: search snippets only; the dissertation bundles inequivalent-count papers and is not an independent source for M(n).
Manifold Markets question on whether D(10) will be known by 2040: a forecast, not evidence.
Jinyoung Park NYU Feb 2025 talk 'Dedekind's Problem and beyond': a talk on the Jenssen et al. result, not a new event.
The Moonlight (themoonlight.io) AI-generated paper reviews of the De Causmaecker and Van Hirtum paper: aggregator summaries, not opened, not treated as checking.
Symja/mathda Dedekind calculator: lists M(10) as unevaluated; not an event.
